name: Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent
history: The traditional calendar joins two martyrs of Milan and two popes on this day. Saint Ambrose found the body of Nazarius in a garden outside Milan in 395, and with it that of the boy Celsus. Victor I, an African, was pope at the end of the second century. Innocent I led the Church in Rome when the city was sacked by the Goths in 410.
life: Paulinus, the biographer of Saint Ambrose, tells how in 395 the bishop uncovered the body of the martyr Nazarius in a garden outside the walls of Milan and carried it to the new church of the Apostles, where he is still honoured. Nearby lay Celsus, whom tradition makes a boy disciple martyred with him; when or how they died is unknown. Victor I, pope around 189 to 199, is said to have been the first Latin-speaking bishop of Rome and tried to make all the churches keep Easter on a Sunday, threatening to cut off the churches of Asia until Saint Irenaeus urged him to patience. He is honoured as a martyr by tradition. Innocent I, pope from 401 to 417, defended Saint John Chrysostom when he was exiled, confirmed the African bishops’ condemnation of Pelagius, and laboured for Rome through the barbarian invasions, being at Ravenna seeking peace when Alaric sacked the city.
prayerTo: Holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, holy popes Victor and Innocent, you served Christ in times of persecution, division and collapse. Pray for the Church in every hard season, for the Pope and the bishops, and for me, that I may stand firm when the world around me falls apart. Amen.
penance: Pray today for the Pope, and for a city or country suffering war or collapse. Give something to help refugees.
meditation: Innocent watched Rome fall and kept the Church steady. When everything feels uncertain, what in your faith stays fixed?
prayer: May the martyrdom of Your Saints Nazarius, Celsus, Victor and Innocent, give us courage, O Lord, and may it give us a help to counter-balance our weakness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
prayerSource: Collect of the day, Roman Missal of 1962
